questions.q: What triggered the Sentinel analytics rule in this capstone's opening incident?
options: An impossible-travel pattern: the same account signing in from Atlanta, then from Eastern Europe nine minutes later
A failed password attempt from a known device
A scheduled task being created on a workstation
An email being forwarded to an external address
questions.explain: The self-join across SigninLogs caught the same UserPrincipalName signing in successfully from two geographically impossible locations within minutes.

questions.q: What specifically confirmed this was a real incident rather than a false positive?
options: No VPN exit node explained the foreign IP, Teresa wasn't traveling, and she confirmed approving an MFA prompt she hadn't requested
The analyst simply trusted the rule firing without any further check
The account had never signed in from Atlanta before
Defender for Endpoint was offline at the time
questions.explain: Triage ruled out explanations (VPN, travel) and a phone call confirmed MFA push fatigue let the second sign-in through.

questions.q: How did the SOC discover that WKSTN-FIN-14 was also compromised?
options: The investigation graph showed the Account entity linked to a Host entity via a Defender for Endpoint alert the original analytics rule never mentioned
A second analytics rule fired specifically for that host
The user reported their laptop was running slowly
It was found by reviewing backup logs
questions.explain: Scoping the incident through the investigation graph, not just the rule that opened it, surfaced the second compromised asset.

questions.q: Why did the analyst capture a memory and disk triage image before isolating WKSTN-FIN-14?
options: Isolating the device would destroy volatile evidence like running processes and network connections
Capturing evidence is only required for compromised accounts, not hosts
Defender for Endpoint requires a triage capture before it can isolate any device
It was not necessary and was done only as a formality
questions.explain: Evidence-safe containment captures volatile data before an action like isolation would wipe it, which Lesson 30's forensics then relies on.

questions.q: What does this lesson mean by 'short-term containment'?
options: An immediate action, like isolating a host or disabling an account, that stops the bleeding without yet removing the root cause
A permanent fix that fully resolves the incident
A delay tactic used only when no evidence has been found
The final step in the incident response lifecycle
questions.explain: Isolating the host and disabling the account stops active harm; eradicating the actual root cause is Lesson 30's work.
